references.text: Wealth does not help on the day of wrath. [ref:Prov 11:4|Proverbs 11:4] warns that wealth is useless when judgment comes, which mirrors Jesus' warning about the one who stores up treasures for themselves without being rich toward God.
[ref:Prov 23:4-5|Proverbs 23:4-5] warns against striving after wealth, for it can suddenly disappear – it makes wings and flies away like an eagle. This underscores the transience of earthly riches.

The Preacher laments that one must leave all their wealth to another who did not work for it ([ref:Eccles 2:18-19|Ecclesiastes 2:18-19]). This is closely tied to the parable of the rich farmer who stored up treasures for himself but never got to enjoy the fruits.

[ref:Eccles 5:10-14|Ecclesiastes 5:10-14] describes the emptiness of loving wealth and possessions, and how one can suddenly lose everything. The rich farmer experiences exactly this emptiness – he stored up treasures without being rich toward God.

[ref:Jer 17:11|Jeremiah 17:11] compares the one who gathers wealth unjustly to a bird that broods over eggs it has not laid – in the midst of life, wealth leaves them. The parallel to the rich farmer who loses everything is clear.

[ref:Hos 2:6-9|Hosea 2:6-9] speaks of Israel failing to recognize God as the giver of all good things. Storing up for oneself without being rich toward God reflects this root sin: forgetting that everything comes from God.

Jesus exhorts in [ref:Matt 6:19-21|Matthew 6:19-21] not to store up treasures on earth, but in heaven, for where your heart is, there your treasure is. This is the most direct parallel to Luke 12:21 – storing up treasures for oneself versus being rich toward God.

[ref:Luk 12:33-34|Luke 12:33-34] follows up with a concrete exhortation: Sell what you have and give to the poor, get yourselves a treasure in heaven that does not run out. This expands on what it means to be "rich toward God".

The parable of the rich man and Lazarus ([ref:Luk 16:19-22|Luke 16:19-22]) illustrates the consequences of living in abundance without caring for others – a living parallel to the warning in Luke 12:21.

Paul exhorts the rich not to set their hope on uncertain wealth, but on God, and to do good and be rich in good deeds ([ref:1 Tim 6:17-19|1 Timothy 6:17-19]). This is a direct explanation of what it means to be "rich toward God".

[ref:Jas 5:1-3|James 5:1-3] warns the rich that their wealth has rotted and their gold is rusted – they have stored up treasures in the last days. This is a strong parallel to the warning against storing up for oneself without being rich toward God.

The church in Laodicea says "I am rich", but is actually poor ([ref:Rev 3:17-18|Revelation 3:17-18]). This contrast between earthly and spiritual wealth illustrates the point in Luke 12:21 about self-deception and false security.
